slides.title: Physical Memory Limits
slides.body:
A program's logical size can exceed installed RAM

Multiprogramming degree is capped by physical RAM size

Why RAM Falls Short?
slides.notes: Now, before introducing the next memory management technique, let's understand the limitations of relying only on physical memory. As programs become larger and multiple applications run simultaneously, RAM alone is often not sufficient. This limits the number of processes that can execute at a time, and even code that is rarely used continues to occupy valuable memory. These challenges led to the need for a more efficient memory management approach.

slides.title: What Is VM
slides.body:
Illusion Of Space
Large programs and multiple applications can exceed available RAM
01
02
03
04
Virtual Memory allows processes to run without being fully loaded into physical memory
It creates an illusion of larger memory by using secondary storage
Only required pages stay in RAM; unused pages remain in swap space/page file
05
This improves memory usage and supports more processes simultaneously
slides.notes:
Let's summarize the idea behind Virtual Memory. Even when a program is larger than the available RAM, 
it can still execute because only the required pages are kept in physical memory.
 The remaining pages are stored in secondary storage, such as the swap space or page file,
 creating the illusion of a much larger memory. This improves memory utilization and allows
 more processes to run concurrently without requiring additional physical RAM.

slides.title: What Is VM
slides.body: Illusion Of Space
slides.notes: Finally, this table highlights how Virtual Memory differs from Physical Memory. Unlike Physical Memory, which is limited by the installed RAM, Virtual Memory provides the illusion of a much larger address space by using both RAM and disk-based backing storage. From the process's perspective, memory appears private and contiguous, even though the operating system manages where the pages are actually stored. This abstraction allows larger programs to execute efficiently without being restricted by the available physical RAM.
tables: Can exceed RAM, limited by address bus width
Appears private and contiguous to process

slides.title: What Is VM
slides.body: Illusion Of Space
slides.notes: Now, the process views its Virtual Memory as a sequence of pages, such as Page 0, Page 1, Page 2, ... Page v. Using the Memory Map, each page is translated to a frame in Physical Memory. If the page is not present in RAM, it is fetched from the disk, the mapping is updated, and execution continues. This creates the illusion of a large, continuous memory space even though the pages may be spread across Physical Memory and secondary storage.

slides.title: What Is VM?
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: think of Virtual Memory using this library analogy. The bookshelf represents the limited RAM, while the City Library represents the much larger secondary storage. Instead of keeping every book on the shelf, the Library Card lets you access any required book from the library whenever needed. Similarly, Virtual Memory allows a process to work with a much larger memory space by keeping only the required pages in RAM and fetching the remaining pages from the disk on demand.

slides.title: VM Mechanism Overview
slides.body:
Paging Plus Disk
Virtual address space still split into fixed-size pages
01
02
03
04
Only actively used pages occupy physical frames right now
Idle pages are parked on disk in swap space

slides.notes: Next, let's understand the basic idea behind Virtual Memory. It still uses Paging, but not all pages are kept in RAM at the same time. Only the pages that are currently needed remain in physical memory, while the remaining pages are temporarily stored in swap space on the disk. An extended Page Table keeps track of whether each page is present in memory or on disk, ensuring the operating system can retrieve it whenever required.

slides.title: Benefits of Virtual Memory
slides.body: Why It Matters
slides.notes: Moving on, Virtual Memory offers several practical advantages by loading only the pages that are actually required. This allows programs to be larger than the available RAM, supports more processes running simultaneously, and improves overall RAM utilization. Since every process has its own virtual address space, it also provides better process isolation. Additionally, the operating system automatically manages page loading, simplifying programming and enabling shared memory for common code when needed.
tables: Program logical size can exceed installed RAM
More processes fit since each loads only its active part
Separate virtual spaces stop one process corrupting another
Only needed pages occupy frames, less memory wasted
OS manages residency automatically, no manual overlays needed
Common code pages can later be mapped by many processes

slides.title: Additional Benefits
slides.body:
Beyond Basic Memory Management
Removes the old must-fit-fully-in-RAM constraint
Frees programmers from manual overlay design used earlier
Enables memory-sharing techniques such as copy-on-write
slides.notes: Next, Virtual Memory offers a few additional advantages beyond efficient RAM utilization. Programs are no longer restricted by the requirement to fit entirely in RAM, allowing much larger applications to execute. It also removes the need for manually designing overlays, as the operating system manages page loading automatically. This mechanism also lays the foundation for advanced memory-sharing techniques like Copy-on-Write, where memory can be shared efficiently until a modification is made.

slides.title: Demand Paging
slides.body:
Load Pages on Demand
Loads a page only when it is first referenced
01
02

This on-demand approach is called lazy loading
Avoids loading unused pages into RAM
Reduces startup time and memory usage

slides.notes: Now, let's look at one of the most important concepts in Virtual Memory—Demand Paging. Instead of loading all pages when a process starts, the operating system brings a page into RAM only when it is actually needed, a technique known as lazy loading. This avoids loading unused pages, reducing both startup time and memory usage, while allowing a process to begin execution even before all of its pages are loaded.

slides.notes: Now, let's see how pages move between Main Memory and the Disk in Demand Paging. Here, Program A and Program B occupy pages in Main Memory. When memory becomes full, the operating system performs a Page out, moving a less frequently used page to the Disk. Later, if that page is needed again, a Page in operation brings it back into RAM. This continuous movement of pages allows multiple programs to execute efficiently, even when physical memory is limited.

slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: Finally, think of Demand Paging like ordering food in a restaurant. The menu represents the program's Virtual Memory, but the chef doesn't prepare every dish in advance. Instead, only when a customer places an order is the required dish prepared and served. Similarly, the operating system loads only the required page from the disk into RAM when it is first requested, avoiding unnecessary memory usage and improving efficiency.

slides.title: Valid vs Invalid Bit
slides.body:
How the MMU Interprets Page Presence
Each page table entry gains one extra bit - the valid-invalid bit - recording whether the page is currently present in a physical frame
MMU checks this bit on every single reference
slides.notes: Next, to determine whether a page is available in RAM, the MMU checks the Valid-Invalid Bit in the Page Table Entry. If the bit is valid, the frame number is used immediately for address translation. If it is invalid, it means the page is either not currently in memory or the address is not allowed, so the MMU raises a trap and hands control to the operating system. This check happens on every memory reference to ensure the requested page is available before access.

slides.title: Valid Invalid Bit
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: A hotel receptionist checks your room key: a valid key opens the room immediately, while an invalid key sends you back to the front desk. Similarly, the valid-invalid bit lets the MMU access a page immediately if it's present, or hands control to the OS if it isn't.

slides.title: Pure Demand Paging
slides.body:
Nothing Preloaded Ever
Process begins execution with zero pages resident
01
02
03
04
Even the first instruction page must fault in
Guarantees at least one fault before any execution
Practical systems often preload a few starting pages
05
Pure form is mainly a theoretical baseline for analysis
slides.notes: Now, let's look at Pure Demand Paging, the extreme form of demand paging. Here, a process starts with no pages loaded in RAM, so even the page containing the first instruction must be brought into memory through a page fault. This guarantees at least one page fault before execution begins. In practice, however, operating systems usually preload a few initial pages to avoid this startup delay, making pure demand paging more of a theoretical reference model than a commonly used approach.

slides.title: Pure vs Practical Demand Paging
slides.body: How the First Instruction Is Loaded
slides.notes: Finally, let's compare Pure and Practical Demand Paging. In Pure Demand Paging, the first instruction is never loaded in advance, so execution always begins with a page fault. In contrast, Practical Demand Paging improves startup performance by preloading the entry pages, allowing the process to begin execution with fewer initial delays. This is why modern operating systems prefer the practical approach over the pure theoretical model.
tables: Always faults, fetched only on first access
OS may preload entry pages for smooth start

slides.body: Page Faults
slides.notes: Next we will learn about the Page Faults

slides.title: Page Fault Trap
slides.body:
Trigger Condition Explained
MMU detects an invalid bit (0) during address translation
01
02
03
04
CPU halts the current instruction, traps to the OS, and switches to kernel mode
The page-fault handler identifies the type of fault
The OS either loads the required page or terminates the process if the reference is invalid
slides.notes: Next, let's see what happens when a Page Fault occurs. During address translation, if the MMU finds the Valid Bit set to 0, it immediately stops the current instruction and transfers control to the operating system by switching to kernel mode. The page-fault handler then checks whether the access is legitimate. If the page simply isn't in RAM, the operating system loads it and resumes execution; otherwise, if the reference is invalid, the process is terminated.

slides.title: Page Fault vs Invalid Access
slides.body: OS Decision Flow
slides.notes:
Moving on, the Valid Bit alone doesn't determine whether an access is a Page Fault or an Invalid Access. 
If the bit is 1, the address is translated normally and execution continues. However, when the bit is 0,
 the operating system checks whether the requested address belongs to the process's logical address space. 
If it does, a genuine Page Fault is serviced by loading the page into RAM; otherwise,
 it is treated as an illegal address, and the process is terminated.

Page legal but absent, service the fault

Fault Resolution Flow

Now, let's walk through the complete Page Fault Resolution Flow. 1 First, the CPU makes a reference, 
and the Page Table indicates that the required page is not present, 2 causing a trap to the Operating System. 
The OS then checks whether the 3  page exists on the backing store. If it does, the missing page is 
4 loaded into a free frame in Physical Memory, after which the Page Table is 5 updated with the new frame information.
 Finally, the 6 interrupted instruction is restarted, allowing the process to continue as if the page had always been in memory.

slides.title: Page Fault Trap
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes:
Finally, think of a Page Fault Trap like a security checkpoint. When the car reaches the checkpoint, 
it cannot continue immediately—it must first go through a check. Similarly, when the MMU detects
 that a required page is not currently available, it raises a trap and hands control to the Operating System. 
After verification, if the request is valid, execution is allowed to continue; otherwise, 
the request is stopped, just like a vehicle that fails the security check.

slides.title: Page Fault Handling Steps
slides.body: OS Process to Load a Missing Page
slides.notes: Now, let's summarize how the operating system handles a Page Fault. 1 It first checks the PCB to confirm that the memory reference is valid and 2 then locates the required page on the disk.3  Next, it finds a free frame in physical memory and reads the missing page into that frame. After loading, 5 the Page Table is updated with the new frame number, and the Valid Bit is set to 1. 6 Finally, the instruction that caused the Page Fault is restarted, allowing the process to continue normally.

Records the frame number, sets valid bit to 1
Re-executes the instruction that originally caused the trap

slides.title: Fault Handling Notes
slides.body:
Key Execution Considerations
Step order is fixed; skipping any step breaks correctness
01
02
03
04
If no free frame exists, a victim must be chosen first
Victim-selection algorithms handle the no-free-frame case separately
Instruction restarts fully, it does not resume mid-way
slides.notes: Finally, it's important to understand that page fault handling follows a fixed sequence, and each step must be completed in order to ensure correct execution. If no free frame is available, the operating system first selects a victim page using a page replacement algorithm before loading the required page. Once the page is available, the interrupted instruction is restarted from the beginning, rather than continuing from where it stopped.

slides.title: Page 4 Fault Trace
slides.body: Step-by-Step Resolution
slides.notes: Now, let's trace the complete resolution of a Page 4 Fault. The MMU first detects that Page 4 has a Valid Bit of 0 and raises a trap. The Operating System confirms that the page is valid but currently resides on the disk. It then allocates the free Frame 11, loads Page 4 into it, and updates the Page Table Entry (PTE) so that Page 4 now points to Frame 11 with the Valid Bit set to 1. Finally, the interrupted instruction is restarted and completes successfully.

slides.title: Page Fault and Multiprogramming
slides.body:
CPU Utilization During Disk I/O
Same steps apply for any page, in any process
01
02
03
04
Process moves to a wait state during the disk read
CPU is free to run another ready process meanwhile
This reuse of CPU time supports strong multiprogramming
slides.notes: Moving on, the page fault handling mechanism works the same regardless of which page or process triggers it. While the required page is being fetched from the disk, the faulting process enters the wait state instead of occupying the CPU. Rather than remaining idle, the operating system schedules another ready process for execution. This efficient use of CPU time is one of the major reasons Virtual Memory and Demand Paging work so well with multiprogramming.

slides.title: Page Fault Service Time
slides.body:
Disk Dominates Cost
Page fault service time is the total time the OS takes to complete all six steps, from the trap firing to the instruction successfully restarting. It has three components, and one of them is far larger than the other two combined
slides.notes: Next, let's understand what Page Fault Service Time actually represents. It is the total time taken from the moment a page fault occurs until the interrupted instruction is restarted successfully. This includes all the steps performed by the operating system, but the disk access time contributes the most to the overall delay, making it the dominant factor in page fault handling.

slides.title: Page Fault Time Components
slides.body: Disk I/O Dominates the Delay
slides.notes: Now, let's examine the three components of Page Fault Service Time. First, the Trap and OS overhead takes only a few microseconds and includes saving the CPU state and executing the page-fault handler. Next comes the Disk I/O Time, which is the most expensive part—typically around 1 to 10 milliseconds on an HDD, as the operating system must locate and transfer the required page into memory. Finally, there's a small restart overhead of a few microseconds to resume the fetch-decode-execute cycle. Since Disk I/O is much slower than the other two components, it dominates the overall page fault delay.
tables: Saving CPU state, running handler decision logic
Roughly 1 to 10 ms on HDD, far less on SSD
Seek, rotate, and transfer the page into the frame

slides.title: Page Fault Performance Impact
slides.body:
Memory vs Disk Access Gap
01
02
03
A single fault costs orders of magnitude more than one memory access
Typical RAM access is around 100 nanoseconds
SSD-backed swap narrows, but does not close, this gap
04
Even one avoidable fault can outweigh many normal accesses
slides.notes: Moving on, a Page Fault is much more expensive than a normal memory access because it involves accessing the disk instead of just RAM. While a typical RAM access takes around 100 nanoseconds, fetching a page from secondary storage takes significantly longer. Even with modern SSDs, this gap remains substantial, which is why avoiding unnecessary page faults is essential for maintaining good system performance.

slides.title: Effective Access Time
slides.body:
Extending EAT Formula
Effective access time (EAT) calculates the average memory access cost. With demand paging, page faults add extra delay with probability p
p = probability a reference causes a page fault
01
02
03
(1 − p) = probability the page is already resident
ma = normal memory access time, no fault
05
EAT = (1 − p) × ma + p × (Page Fault Service Time + ma)
04
Page fault service time = time to handle the fault and load the page
slides.notes: Next, let's extend the Effective Access Time (EAT) formula to include Demand Paging. Here, p represents the probability of a page fault, while 1−p represents the probability that the required page is already present in RAM. If no page fault occurs, only the normal memory access time (ma) is incurred. However, when a page fault occurs, the Page Fault Service Time is added before the memory access can complete. This formula helps us calculate the average memory access time by considering both situations together.

slides.title: EAT Worked Example
slides.body:
Calculating Real Slowdown
Take a typical machine with memory access time ma equal to 200 nanoseconds and an average page fault service time of 8 milliseconds, a realistic value once disk seek and transfer are included. Suppose the fault rate p is 0.001, meaning one in every thousand references faults
slides.notes: Now, let's apply the EAT formula using a practical example. Here, the normal memory access time (ma) is 200 nanoseconds, the Page Fault Service Time is 8 milliseconds, and the page fault probability (p) is 0.001, which means one out of every 1000 memory references results in a page fault. In the next step, we'll substitute these values into the formula to calculate the Effective Access Time and observe how even a very small page fault rate can significantly impact overall performance.

slides.title: Effective Access Time Analysis
slides.body: Page Fault Impact
slides.notes: Now, let's interpret the result of the calculation. Without any page faults, a memory access takes only 200 nanoseconds. However, with a page fault probability of just 0.001—that is, one fault in every 1000 references—the Effective Access Time increases to about 8.2 microseconds. This is roughly a 41× slowdown, showing that even a very small page fault rate can significantly affect overall system performance because disk access is much slower than RAM.

slides.title: Acceptable Fault Rate
slides.body:
Keeping Slowdown Small
How small must p be to keep EAT within 10% of the no-fault time? With ma = 200 ns and service time = 8 ms, the target EAT ≤ 220 ns gives p ≤ 0.0000025 - about one fault in every 400,000 references
slides.notes: Finally, let's determine what constitutes an acceptable page fault rate. To keep the Effective Access Time within just 10% of the normal 200 ns memory access time, the page fault probability must be extremely smallp≤0.0000025, which is about one page fault in every 400,000 memory references. Compare this with the earlier example of p=0.001, or one fault in every 1,000 references, which resulted in a 41× slowdown. This highlights why operating systems strive to keep the page fault rate as low as possible.

slides.title: Reducing Page Fault Rate
slides.body:
Keeping p Low
Fault rate must stay extremely low for good performance
01
02
03
04
Strong locality of reference keeps p naturally low
Enough allocated frames per process also reduces p
Fast SSD-backed swap shrinks damage per fault, not p itself
slides.notes: Moving on, the key to achieving good Virtual Memory performance is keeping the page fault rate (p) as low as possible. This is naturally achieved when programs exhibit locality of reference, repeatedly accessing the same set of pages. Allocating a sufficient number of frames to each process further reduces page faults, while using a faster SSD-backed swap only decreases the time taken to service a fault—it does not reduce the fault rate itself.

slides.title: Why Copy On Write
slides.body:
Fork Duplication Problem
The fork() system call creates a child process by giving it a copy of the parent's entire address space. Copying every page - code, stack, heap and data - byte for byte is expensive, and most of that work turns out to be wasted
The waste is severe: most children call exec() right after fork(), discarding the just-copied address space to load a fresh program. Duplicating megabytes only to throw it away microseconds later is the inefficiency to avoid
slides.notes: Now, let's understand why Copy-on-Write (COW) was introduced. During a fork() call, the child process is initially given a copy of the parent's entire address space, including the code, data, heap, and stack. Creating this complete copy is expensive, especially because most child processes immediately execute exec(), replacing the copied memory with a new program. As a result, a large amount of copying effort is wasted, and Copy-on-Write was designed to eliminate this unnecessary duplication.

slides.title: Traditional Fork Overhead
slides.body:
Why Copying Is Wasteful
Traditional fork() copies every page of parent memory
01
02
03
04
Copying is proportional to process size, can be slow
Most children call exec() right after forking
exec() replaces the address space almost immediately
05
Nearly all of that copied memory is never used
slides.notes: Next, let's look at why the traditional fork() approach is inefficient. It creates a complete copy of the parent's address space, so the time taken increases with the size of the process. However, in most cases, the child process immediately invokes exec(), which replaces the entire copied address space with a new program. This means that almost all the copied memory is never actually used, resulting in unnecessary overhead.

slides.title: Traditional Fork Overhead
slides.body: Full Memory Copy Cost
slides.notes: Now, this table summarizes the drawbacks of the traditional full-copy fork() approach. Since the entire address space is copied, the fork() operation becomes slower as the process size increases and the memory requirement almost doubles immediately. If the child process then calls exec(), that copied memory is discarded, making the entire copying effort unnecessary. This inefficiency is exactly what Copy-on-Write aims to eliminate.
tables: Doubles, parent plus full child copy

slides.title: Copy-On-Write Mechanism
slides.body:
How Read-Only Sharing Works?
fork() only duplicates page tables, not page contents
01
02
03
04
Shared frames marked read-only for both processes
Reads from either process proceed with no restriction
A write attempt raises a write-protection fault
slides.notes: Next, let's see how Copy-on-Write (COW) avoids unnecessary memory copying. Instead of duplicating the actual pages, fork() initially copies only the page tables, allowing both parent and child to share the same physical memory. These shared pages are marked read-only, so both processes can continue performing read operations normally. Only when either process attempts to write to a shared page does a write-protection fault occur, allowing the operating system to create a separate copy only when it's actually needed.

slides.notes: Next, notice that a new copy of the page is not created as soon as a write occurs. Instead, the operating system creates a private copy only for the process that is modifying the data, while the other process continues using the original shared page. This selective copying is what makes Copy-on-Write both memory-efficient and faster than the traditional fork() approach.

slides.notes: In Copy-on-Write, both Process A and Process B initially share the same Page X in read-only mode, so no extra frames are allocated. Only when Process A performs a write does the Write Trigger create a separate Page X′ (Copy), while Process B continues using the original Page X. This lazy copying makes Copy-on-Write much more memory-efficient.

slides.title: Memory-Mapped Files
slides.body:
Files As Memory
A memory-mapped file (mmap()) maps a file into virtual memory, allowing access through normal memory operations instead of read() and write()
Memory-mapped files use demand paging: file pages are loaded only on first access, with the valid-invalid bit tracking page presence
slides.notes: Now, let's look at another important application of Virtual Memory—Memory-Mapped Files. Instead of accessing a file using read() and write() system calls, the operating system maps the file directly into the process's virtual memory, allowing it to be accessed just like normal memory. Since this mapping uses Demand Paging, only the required file pages are loaded on first access, with the Valid-Invalid Bit indicating whether a page is currently present in RAM.

slides.notes: Next, Memory-Mapped Files provide both efficiency and easy data sharing. Since they use Demand Paging, file pages are brought into RAM only when they are first accessed through a page fault. The same file can also be mapped into the address spaces of multiple processes, and with MAP_SHARED, changes made by one process become visible to the others. Behind the scenes, the operating system manages these file-backed pages using the same demand-paging mechanism as regular virtual memory.

The physical frames are backed by the Disk File, which also contains pages 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5. This means the operating system keeps only one copy of the file in Physical Memory, allowing both processes to access the same data efficiently without creating duplicate copies.

slides.title: Memory-Mapped Files Comparison
slides.body: mmap() vs Traditional I/O
slides.notes: Moving on, this comparison highlights the main difference between traditional I/O and mmap(). With traditional read() and write(), every file operation requires an explicit system call, and the data is copied through a kernel buffer before reaching the process. In contrast, mmap() maps the file directly into the process's virtual memory, reducing data copying and enabling multiple processes to share the same physical frames. As a result, traditional I/O is generally suitable for small sequential reads, whereas mmap() is more efficient for large files or applications with frequent random access.
